title: the Sri Sukta
hook: a junk drawer, a sink full of dishes, and a hymn that gives misfortune a face and shows it the door

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sri Sukta named her tree, the bilva, born from her own tapas. What hard-shelled task did you crack open? Today, the hymn meets the one it wants gone. Day one thousand ninety-seven.

A home can have a corner that sags. The junk drawer that won't close. The sink that's been full since Tuesday. The pile of mail nobody wants to open. None of it is a disaster. But walk into a room like that when you're already tired, and something heavy can settle on the shoulders. The Sri Sukta has a name for that heaviness, and it isn't shy about it. A few lines ago the singer asked for misfortune to be gone. Today the hymn describes her, and then rolls up its sleeves.
screen: `THE DRAWER THAT WON'T CLOSE.` → `THE SINK FULL SINCE TUESDAY.` → `A NAME FOR THE HEAVINESS.`

segments.voice: First, a short stop on the way. Just before this, the hymn asks for a friend of the gods to come with fame and a jewel; tradition hears Kubera there, keeper of treasure. Then the line this day is about, in paraphrase. Hunger and thirst and grime, the elder one, Alakshmi: I drive her away. Non-prosperity, lack, all of it, push it out of my house. Start with her name. Alakshmi is the hymn's word for misfortune, the shadow of Lakshmi. And look at what she's made of. Not curses or monsters. Hunger. Thirst. Dirt. The ordinary signs of a house that's struggling. Then the word elder. The hymn calls her the elder one. Tradition says, in later tellings, that Alakshmi is Lakshmi's older sister, and some honor her as a goddess in her own right, under the name Jyeshtha, the elder. The hymn itself just gives the word and moves on. Now notice the grammar, because it's the surprise. The first verb is I. I drive her away. For once, the singer isn't only asking. He takes part. Then he turns back to the goddess: you, push the rest out of my house. Some readers hear a partnership in that: the person sweeps, and grace finishes the work. Others hear the hymn's plain realism. Fortune in this hymn lives in a household, and a household has dishes and floors and a pantry to keep. Either way, misfortune here isn't a fate from the sky. It's something with a face and an address, and the singer is willing to show it the door.
screen: `A FRIEND OF THE GODS, WITH A JEWEL.` · `HUNGER, THIRST AND GRIME.` · `ALAKSHMI, THE ELDER ONE.` · `I DRIVE HER AWAY; YOU FINISH IT.` · then, large: `MISFORTUNE HAS AN ADDRESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one corner. Settle, and let the breath slow. In your mind, walk through your home until you find the corner that sags: the drawer, the sink, the pile, the inbox. Don't scold yourself. Just look at it honestly. Then picture it clear. One surface, empty and wiped. Feel what that would be like to walk past. Breathe there for a while. If you pray, you can ask the goddess, or God, for help with the part you can't do alone. If you don't, simply decide which small part is yours. The bell holds the time.
The Sri Sukta. A hymn that names Alakshmi, the elder one, made of hunger, thirst and grime, and says: I drive her away; you push the rest out of my house.
Your line: the Sri Sukta. Today, clear one corner of your home completely, just one, and notice how it feels to walk past it. Day one thousand ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Some Hindu households clean the house thoroughly before Diwali and Lakshmi worship, and some describe it as clearing Alakshmi out before welcoming Lakshmi in.

original.note: Sanskrit: alakṣmīm, misfortune, named in the Sri Sukta as the elder one to be driven out.

trapdoor: what you thought: misfortune is just bad luck that falls on you.
what it means: the hymn gives misfortune a face, Alakshmi, made of hunger, thirst and grime, and the singer helps show her the door.
what a scholar hears: kṣutpipāsāmalāṃ jyeṣṭhām alakṣmīṃ nāśayāmy aham: 'the elder' here, and in later tradition Jyeshtha, Lakshmi's elder sister, honored as a goddess herself.

sources.ref: Sri Sukta, verses 7–8 (Rig Veda khila, as commonly recited)

notes: Verse 8 paraphrased: kṣutpipāsāmalāṃ jyeṣṭhām alakṣmīṃ nāśayāmy aham / abhūtim asamṛddhiṃ ca sarvāṃ nirṇuda me gṛhāt. nāśayāmi is first person ('I destroy / I drive away'); nirṇuda is imperative. The script rests on this shift; confirm the reading.
Verse 7 (upaitu māṃ devasakhaḥ kīrtiś ca maṇinā saha) mentioned briefly; 'devasakha' as Kubera is a traditional reading, attributed to tradition. Confirm.

Alakshmi as Lakshmi's elder sister and Jyeshtha as a goddess in her own right are later Puranic and regional traditions, attributed to 'later tradition'. Jyeshtha glossed 'the elder' (lexical). Confirm.
howItsDone: Diwali cleaning described as clearing out Alakshmi is a practice some households describe; confirm wording.
'A few lines ago the singer asked for misfortune to be gone' refers to verse 5 (day 1095).

Editor pass: hook's 'in a lot of homes' (sweeping claim) changed to 'a home can have'; the Alakshmi-as-elder-sister and Jyeshtha lines recast as 'tradition says, in later tellings' and 'some honor her', since verse 8 only gives the word jyeṣṭhā.
